author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Bridge with Too Many Owners
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The bridge had three names and no maintenance budget.

In Tideglass we called it the canal crossing. People from Riverstone called it the east span. Brasswatch's invoices referred to it as Structural Link R-4, which made Toph laugh so hard she nearly fell off the bench.

"Wonderful," she said. "If it collapses, we can file a complaint with the alphabet."

Tamsin did not laugh. She had the inspection report spread out in front of her, and the numbers were unpleasant.

The eastern handrail needed replacement. The expansion joint had swollen after the last flood. A support near Sela's vegetable garden still required monitoring. Riverstone had paid for most of the original construction, but Tideglass used the crossing to bring fish and coastal herbs to market. Brasswatch's carts brought tools over it. Jasmine Steps depended on it when the upper delivery road was closed.

Everybody used the bridge.

Nobody had agreed who would pay to keep it safe.

Aang studied the report. Katara stood beside him with the water delivery schedule. Toph had both feet on the ground, listening to movement through the old stone foundation. Edda sat near the door, positioned where she could see the drawings without asking someone to hold them up.

Maui leaned toward me.

"I could repair the rail."

"You could," I whispered. "Then who checks it next year?"

He sighed.

That was the question that ruined every easy solution.

The committee meeting began with a disagreement about jurisdiction. A Riverstone representative said that a bridge built with local funds belonged to Riverstone. Fen replied that tidal water carried the risk from Tideglass. Danse argued that anyone sending heavy carts over the span should contribute to the wear. A market vendor protested that they could barely afford transport fees already.

Sela stood up.

"My garden flooded because someone moved a cart path without checking the drainage. I don't care who owns the bridge on paper. I want the next repair to include the water under it."

Toph nodded.

"Finally, a person asking about the ground."

Aang tried to settle the room. He had a calm, earnest voice, and people liked listening to the Avatar. I could see him beginning to offer a neat compromise before the affected residents had finished speaking.

Katara touched his arm.

"Let them finish."

He stopped.

It was a small thing, and it changed the meeting.

Edda described how the alternate route became too steep after rain. A cart driver explained why heavier loads were being diverted to the ridge, increasing delivery times. Mara laid out the pantry's costs. Fen showed tide marks from the last storm. Nobody had the whole answer.

I took notes, then realized I was writing the same word on every page.

*Owner.*

I crossed it out and wrote *responsibility.*

When the discussion broke for lunch, Maui found me beside the notice board.

"Are they going to argue all day?"

"Probably."

"What if I pay for the rail myself?"

"That would pay for the rail."

"It would help."

"Yes. But then everyone would wait for you the next time it broke."

He looked toward the bridge.

"I don't want that."

"Then help them make a plan they can keep without you."

We returned after lunch.

I asked whether the committee would consider a shared maintenance ledger. It would record which districts used the crossing, what loads passed over it, what inspections were due, and what each district could contribute without pretending their resources were equal. Urgent repairs would be funded from a shared reserve, but the reserve's rules would be public.

The idea was not greeted with enthusiasm.

"More paperwork," Toph said.

"More accurate paperwork," I answered.

"Still paperwork."

Danse smiled faintly.

We spent two hours negotiating what counted as a fair contribution. The final proposal did not divide the cost equally by district. The market and pantry would pay lower fees for essential deliveries, while heavier commercial transport contributed more toward wear. Riverstone would maintain the public approach. Brasswatch would provide scheduled technical inspections, with workers paid. Tideglass would monitor flood and salt exposure. The council would review the arrangement after the first storm season.

Nobody got everything they wanted.

That was probably why it was worth trying.

When the vote came, the proposal passed narrowly.

The bridge remained closed until the repairs and inspections were complete.

I felt disappointed, though I had argued for the restriction myself. People needed the crossing now. The idea that being responsible could still mean waiting was hard to bear.

After the meeting, Toph came to find me.

"You looked like you swallowed a bucket of sand," she said.

"That was roughly how the vote felt."

"You got your ledger."

"We got a process. The bridge is still closed."

She tapped her heel against the floor.

"Stone doesn't care if the vote was popular. It cares whether the support holds."

I smiled.

"That sounds like you."

"It is me."

Maui joined us carrying two cups of tea. He handed one to Toph.

She sniffed it.

"From Iroh?"

"Yes."

"Then you're forgiven for whatever you did before lunch."

He laughed.

We walked toward the bridge at dusk. The closure signs glowed beneath the lanterns, and the water moved through its temporary channel. Aang and Katara were still discussing the delivery schedule nearby. Edda checked the path with Pip before turning toward home.

Maui slipped his arm around my shoulders.

"You're tired."

"I am."

"Can I make you dinner?"

"Only if you promise not to rebuild the kitchen."

"I promise nothing."

I looked up at him.

He grinned.

"Fine. I promise."

We walked home as the first evening tide touched the low stones. The bridge had too many names, perhaps, but its responsibilities were finally written down.

That was a beginning.

Not a magnificent one.

A useful one.
